title: AEO benchmarking: What market data reveals about AI search
content:
AEO benchmarking measures your brand’s AI search visibility against competitors and market trends. It tells you whether a change in your visibility comes from the market or from your own brand, so you can prove performance to leadership before you change tactics.
Your AI visibility drops this week, and you can’t tell whether ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity changed how they answer or your content slipped. Without a benchmark, every dip looks like your fault — and every spike looks like your win.
AEO benchmarking is the practice of comparing your brand’s visibility in answer engines against a reference point: competitors, an industry baseline, or your own history. If you’ve done competitive benchmarking in other channels, the logic is the same. You measure against peers on consistent metrics so a number like “38% visibility” carries meaning. The channel is what changes. Instead of rankings and clicks, you measure how often ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity mention and cite your brand.
Together, these create an accountability gap. Organic traffic can fall while rankings hold, because the answer appears above the links. Leadership asks what changed, and without a benchmark you can’t separate a market shift from a brand-specific issue.
Pro tip: Treat every unexplained change as two questions. What happened to the market? What happened to us? Benchmarking answers the first so you can focus on the second.
The two-tier model pairs market-wide benchmarks with brand-level performance data. It’s how you benchmark your AI search performance against your industry: read the external trend first, then your internal KPIs.
AI Search Sensor provides market-wide AEO benchmarks. It’s a free dashboard (currently in beta) covering ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity. HubSpot AEO measures brand-level AI visibility performance, and teams on Marketing Hub Pro or Enterprise get AEO included. AI Search Sensor pairs with HubSpot AEO for two-tier AEO measurement.
A single tier misleads in both directions. Brand-only data can’t show whether a drop is yours or everyone’s. Market-only data can’t show whether you’re keeping pace. Comparing the two before you change tactics prevents the most expensive AEO mistake: fixing a problem that isn’t yours.
HubSpot’s AEO case study shows benchmarking first in practice. Benchmark data revealed significant Reddit citation growth in German and French markets with zero HubSpot mentions. After a localized campaign, HubSpot’s mention rate rose from 0% to 33.5% in France and 17.1% in Germany within one month.
AEO benchmarking measures four things across AI engines: citation rate, share of voice, sentiment, and citation/source attribution. Each answers a different diagnostic question.
The citation rate formula comes from Stackmatix’s September 2026 measurement guide . AI Search Sensor reports two related market benchmarks: visibility score (how often a brand is mentioned relative to other tracked brands, 0 to 100%) and citation share (how often a brand’s domain appears among all citations analyzed).
Share of voice shows how prominent you are relative to competitors. If 100 brand mentions appear across you and your competitors and 25 are yours, your share of voice is 25%. It’s the metric most likely to explain why a competitor gets named in buying conversations, and you don’t.
Sentiment shows whether engines describe your brand favorably, and it connects directly to your brand health . If sentiment falls while visibility holds, you have a perception problem rather than a discovery problem, and the fix differs.
Source attribution shows where engines get their information about you, and it often points off your own site. In AI Search Sensor ’s Top Citation Domain Analysis, NerdWallet and Bankrate out-cite Bank of America and JPMorgan combined in Financial Services (HubSpot, updated October 2026, based on 50 representative HubSpot AEO portals). When third parties shape your category’s answers, your own blog can’t move the number alone.
Topic coverage is the share of your priority topics where your brand appears at all. Entity alignment is whether engines describe your brand, products, and pricing accurately, which Stackmatix tracks as brand mention accuracy. Market benchmarks don’t show either one, so they belong in your internal tier.
A reliable AEO benchmark depends on three design choices: which prompts you track, how often you run them, and which engines you cover.
A prompt cohort is a fixed set of prompts that you run the same way over time. Prompt cohorts improve benchmark reliability through consistent coverage. An ad hoc query set, where you test whatever question comes to mind, can’t show trends because week-to-week results aren’t comparable.
Build the cohort around intent. Stackmatix recommends 50 to 100 prompts organized by topic cluster and intent type, covering category, brand-adjacent, and direct brand questions.
Pro tip: Check out more market research tools and resources that can help you source category questions and competitive context.
Run the same cohort on the same schedule. Weekly is a practical default and matches the weekly rhythm of AI Search Sensor’s traffic and citation data. Keep engines, prompt wording, and settings fixed, and label any change so a method shift doesn’t look like a market shift.
AI answers vary from run to run, so one sample can mislead. A 2026 paper by Ronald Sielinski sampled Perplexity, OpenAI’s SearchGPT, and Google Gemini repeatedly. It found unstable citation rankings and many apparent domain differences inside the noise floor, and it recommends reporting uncertainty estimates.
If you’re new to the concept, this guide to statistical significance explains why small gaps often mean nothing. Stackmatix reaches a similar conclusion and recommends 30 to 60 day trend windows over point-in-time snapshots.
AI Search Sensor is a free tool that benchmarks AI visibility, citations, and traffic by industry, and you can test it below. Paid options exist too. Stackmatix’s guide compares platforms such as Scrunch AI, Otterly AI, Semrush’s AI Toolkit, and Ahrefs Brand Radar. For market context, start with the widget.
That order applies the two-tier model: external market signal first, then internal brand performance.
What we like: AI Search Sensor publishes its methodology. Industry benchmarks use four representative companies per industry, built from public information. Traffic, citation, and volatility charts use anonymized HubSpot customer data.
To tell whether answer engine behavior is shifting across the market right now, check the volatility score, then compare it with your own metrics. The AI Search Sensor compares daily mention rate, citation rate, citation type, and AI-referred traffic against rolling averages. A spike means the engines changed. Market-wide benchmark changes help diagnose external AI shifts versus brand-specific performance issues.
In the first, your visibility falls during a week when volatility reads Elevated. Wait a week, gather more data, and report it as a market event.
In the second, your visibility falls during a Calm week while a competitor’s share of voice climbs. That points to your brand, and a content audit is justified.
Both scenarios prevent the same false alarm: rewriting content to fix a change that content didn’t cause.
An AEO benchmarking action plan sorts findings into two buckets: actions the evidence supports and hypotheses that need testing.
Conclusions from a single week of data, and explanations for why an engine favors a format, are hypotheses. Test them on a limited set of pages, then watch your cohort for several weeks before scaling.
Lead with the two-tier comparison: what the market did, what you did, and the gap. Label which conclusions are evidence and which are hypotheses. Leadership trusts a team that states its uncertainty.
Comparable AEO benchmarks require governance. The practical version is a short checklist:
Start with 50 to 100 prompts organized by topic cluster and intent. That range, recommended by Stackmatix, covers category, comparison, and brand questions. Smaller cohorts work for pilots but produce noisier results, so keep the set stable and trend it over several weeks.
Track ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity first. AI Search Sensor and HubSpot AEO both cover these three, so your brand data and market data line up on the same engines. Add Google AI Overviews and others once your core workflow is steady.
Run it weekly. Weekly cadence matches the rhythm of AI Search Sensor’s market data and gives you enough points to see a trend. Review monthly for strategy, and judge change over 30 to 60 day windows rather than single days.
Map each finding to a content decision. Citation share by content type shows which formats to publish, competitor prompt gaps show which topics to cover, and channel data shows where off-site work belongs. Rank the list by evidence strength and put hypotheses behind a test.
Show the market trend and your trend side by side, then state what you know and what you’re testing. If volatility was Elevated or Extreme when your numbers moved, say so, and hold off on claiming credit or blame until you have several weeks of data.
Ready to see where the market stands? Get the data behind these benchmarks in the State of AEO report.

title: How to use AI to write a blog post (that isn’t slop)
content:
Like a hammer or even a hair dryer, AI is just a tool. It needs to be wielded skillfully by an expert to achieve greatness. And in a world increasingly full of “AI slop,” this is especially true when exploring how to use AI to write a blog post.
When using AI to write blog posts, you can’t just sit back and click copy-paste and publish. You need to create a thorough brief, build an outline, draft one section at a time, and then edit with the emotion, lived experience, and discernment only a human can.
Despite the popularity of AI-assisted content creation, 62.7% of marketers admit brands need more unique, human-centered content to compete. Google agrees , saying AI can help with research and structure, but you should fact-check and review everything by hand before you publish, as it can get facts wrong.
AI can produce quantity, no doubt, but its quality is up for debate — at least without your guidance. AI is wonderful for structure and first drafts, but only you can bring the expertise, voice, and final quality assurance that produces great content. And this guide will show you how.
You’ll get a five-step process for creating blog posts with AI, human-review checkpoints, prompt templates, and tips for keeping your voice and avoiding the “slop” label .
Generative AI is powerful and useful. It can analyze information and produce materials faster than any human could by hand, which is likely why 80% of marketers now use AI for content creation in some form.
But I’d argue we’re crossing into “too much of a good thing” territory when it comes to generative AI, and I’m not alone. Our research shows that more than half of marketers say AI has made content creation so easy that they are now struggling to stand out in a heavily saturated market.
AI has also faced concerns around plagiarism, bias, data privacy, and inaccuracy for several years. Add its now-mainstream accessibility, and the formulaic output has earned an unsavory nickname, “AI slop.”
AI slop is low-quality, mass-produced digital content created using generative AI with little to no human input or creative thought. (I’m sure you’ve seen the fliers .)
Users and businesses sharing it have been ridiculed as low-effort, unoriginal, or even “fake.” Harsh, yes, but also easy to avoid.
Listen: It’s easy to get caught up in the speed and “polished” finished products that AI generates in seconds; I don’t blame anyone. But at this point, we, as marketers and consumers, have seen enough of its generic output to know we need to do better.
AI is a collaborator, not a replacement for your judgment, creativity, experience, or effort.
Now, I know what many of you are thinking: “Why would I do all that work when AI can do it for me?” And I get it. You want to save time and labor, but to quote former Director of the HubSpot Blog Karla Hesterberg : “The only truly effortless [AI] process produces slop.”
Producing high-quality content with AI — content that delivers real value, builds trust with your audience, ranks well in search engines and answer engines, and closes qualified buyers — requires human effort and insight. It requires human knowledge and input to produce something new and extraordinary.
I’m not saying don’t use AI. I’m saying use your skill with it.
This is something we learned firsthand by adopting AI into our editorial process at HubSpot , and it heavily influenced the steps in this guide. Tools like HubSpot’s brand voice and AI content writer were built with this all in mind.
AI is like an eager new intern. It’s fast and takes direction, but it doesn’t have your lived expertise or knowledge of your customer, data, and standards. The steps we share in this guide are designed to compensate for that and ensure you maintain your brand voice.
Each step has something you give AI, a choice you make, something you get back, and a moment when a human steps in, based on my decade as a content editor and strategist.
You can follow these steps in common tools like Claude or ChatGPT, or in HubSpot, which offers multiple options.
HubSpot’s free AI Content Writer can draft blog posts, outlines, and more inside the tools you already use. For a full blog workflow, Content Agent builds blog posts, social content, and landing pages in your brand voice. It lives in Agent Hub , which is included in Starter, Professional, and Enterprise editions.
Now that you know what you need, let’s break down our five steps.
Before you turn to an AI content creation tool, you need the right input. Think of these as the creative brief you send an intern.
The “data privacy” point is worth calling out. The U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology lists data privacy as one of 12 risks that are unique to or worse with generative AI . The risk includes leaks of personal or sensitive data. Check your company’s AI policy first.
If you use HubSpot, Agent Hub runs on your CRM data. HubSpot says its third-party AI providers are contractually barred from training on your data. You also control what AI can access. You can read how it works in the HubSpot Trust Center .
Pro tip: Put all your consistent inputs (e.g., brand voice, company history) on a one-pager and save it as a template you can reuse for every post. This saves you time and maintains consistency across different editors.
Need a blog topic? Try HubSpot’s free Blog Idea Generator to spark ideas, then pick the one that fits your goal.
An outline is the heading and talking points plan that AI follows. Skip it, and drafts wander. Start with your brief of inputs. Then ask AI to turn it into an outline. Pair each heading with the reader’s question it answers and the source that supports it.
To get an outline you can actually use, get specific. The more ambiguity you leave, the more likely the finished product will miss the mark.
Look at the difference between a vague prompt and a specific prompt.
Try entering your topic in HubSpot’s free AI Content Writer and asking for an outline. Then edit the headings to match your brief.
Want more prompt ideas? Our guide to writing AI prompts shows how specific details lead to better results.
Once you have a solid outline, you can work with AI to generate the main sections of your article.
You wouldn’t just give a new intern a brief and say “go,” right? You’d likely have them complete the assignment in small chunks to make sure they’re on the right track. Approach A the same way.
Draft sections one by one to increase focus and maintain quality, or even better, draft select sections rather than all of them. Review each one in depth (more on that in the next section). Then move on to the next.
With challenges like plagiarism and inaccuracy, this chunked approach to writing a blog post with AI is worth the effort.
Personally, I prefer to use AI-generated copy simply as a very rough example that gets my creative juices flowing. I edit and revise to fit my own voice, adding my original thoughts, knowledge, and examples, among other things.
You can follow this drafting workflow in Content Hub , HubSpot’s content marketing software. The free AI Content Writer lets you enter a prompt or use slash commands to generate text on demand. Highlight a paragraph, and you can ask it to edit or rephrase the copy.
Pro tip: Content Agent , currently in beta, builds blog posts, LinkedIn content, and landing pages from a single starting point. It researches competitors, pulls keyword data, and loads your brand voice before it writes. For more on where AI helps most in blogging, see our guide to AI writing tools for blogging .
But remember: Drafts written in chunks still need human editing.
Even your best human-written draft shouldn’t be published without thorough editing. Trust, quality, and originality are ensured in the edit, and that goes double for AI-assisted blog posts.
Before anything goes live, have a human team member check four key things:
AI has a way of sounding extra confident, even when it’s wrong.
Heck — Most tools even come with a disclaimer like this one from ChatGPT admitting it “can make mistakes.”
Google says this is because generative models predict a likely sequence of words instead of retrieving facts. So, the output can contain errors, or what we call “hallucinations.” NIST, the U.S. standards agency, lists this risk (it calls it “confabulation”) among the 12 risks associated with generative AI .
Fact-check and review all AI-generated content before you publish. Here’s a routine you can use for every draft:
For high-stakes topics (i.e., legal, medical, financial, or anything that names a specific person or company), add a second reviewer. People can slip up, too, and when it comes to risky subject matter, it’s wise to double-check.
Original means more than not copied. It means your content adds something new. AI-generated content, by its very nature, is derivative, so editing is a must to deliver fresh value.
Edits can be important for ownership, too. In January 2025, the U.S. Copyright Office said that AI-generated output can be protected by copyright only if a human author contributed enough of the expressive elements. Writing prompts doesn’t count. Creative arrangement and modification can, but “enough” leaves a lot of ambiguity. Ask your legal team about your specific situation.
Before you publish any AI-assisted content, run through these checks:
AI doesn’t know your customers, numbers, or stories. You do. That’s why adding first-hand research, case studies, or examples to support AI-assisted blog posts is a powerful way to make them more original.
This matters for search, too. Google’s Search Quality Rater Guidelines flag main content made with little effort, originality, or added value. Your data and examples are the added value.
Including unexpected examples is one of my favorite ways to add originality and personality to my articles. I mean, come on: how often do you see Bollywood mentioned in marketing blogs?
For more edits that make AI drafts sound human, see our guide to humanizing AI content .
More than anything, make sure that your AI-assisted content is true and consistent with your brand voice and perspective.
Using language or sharing opinions that contradict what your brand has already established can cause confusion, and any confusion about your brand’s beliefs can lead to distrust.
To help maintain your brand when using AI to write a blog post, create a voice profile. A voice profile is a short description of how you write and what you sound like. Think of it as a style guide you include in every prompt.
Explain industry jargon or acronyms the first time they appear.
Avoid: “game-changer,” “unlock,” “in today’s fast-paced world.”
HubSpot’s Brand Voice learns your style from your writing samples and generates this guide for you. After that, you can export it to share with AI tools or have it automatically apply your style in supported tools, such as Marketing Hub. You can also set up a brand voice using AI , then fine-tune its personality and tone. Features can vary by plan, so check what your subscription includes.
Need a deeper dive? See our guide on AI brand voice training .
Whether you’re writing by hand or by AI, write for readers first, then polish for search and answer engines. Thankfully, they aren’t dramatically different. Google’s guide to AI search features says AI features are built on the same core ranking and quality systems as traditional search. So, you just need a clear, useful, well-organized post. Here’s how that looks tactically.
People skim; so do search and AI systems. Make your post easy to scan by:
Litmus is a great example of skimmable formatting in action.
AI is a handy assistant for small, repetitive SEO tasks. Ask it for options to edit for:
For a deeper walkthrough of search intent, structure, internal links, and measurement, see our guide to blogging for SEO .
You’ve drafted, edited, and optimized for getting found. Now it’s time to publish. Check your final boxes in four main steps.
1. Do a final check. Read the whole post once, start to finish, as a reader would. Look for voice slips, vague claims, and broken links, and edit as needed. Then confirm the basics:
2. Decide on disclosure. Some teams add a short note on how AI was used in their writing process. Google says sharing how content was created can give readers helpful context and set expectations. Check your company policy and local rules first. (See the FAQ below.)
3. Publish & measure what matters. In HubSpot’s 2026 State of Marketing report , measuring ROI was the top challenge, cited by 33% of respondents. So, keep it simple. Pick three numbers that reflect your goals. A good baseline to consider:
HubSpot can show many of these in one place with its marketing analytics . To see how your brand shows up in AI answers, try the free AEO Grader or HubSpot AEO , currently in beta.
Turn those repeat edits into new rules in your voice profile. Your next draft will start closer to being done.
Ready to put this process into action ? Try HubSpot’s AI Content Writer to draft your next post, then follow the five steps above to make it yours.
Below is a series of prompts that work with HubSpot’s AI Content Writer and most other AI tools. Replace everything in [brackets] before you send, but remember that whatever you get back is just a starting point.
All AI-generated content needs to be reviewed with a human touch to deliver unique value and achieve your long-term search and sales goals. This is especially true when using public prompt templates, as AI tools generally produce the same results for the same inputs.
Every prompt needs your audience, your goal, your approved sources, and your voice profile. Without them, you’ll get generic results. So, include this block before you start drafting anything:
Audience: [who they are and what they already know]
Approved sources: [paste links or notes. Use only these.]
Using the details above, create a one-page brief for a blog post about [topic]. Include the reader’s main question, the angle, a two-sentence direct answer, an outline with H2s and H3s, and the approved source that supports each section. Flag anything the sources don’t support.
Give me three outline options for a [word count] blog post about [topic]. Each H2 must answer one reader question. Put the direct answer first. Don’t add sections that the approved sources can’t support.
Write the section titled “[H2 heading]” in [150-250] words. Use short sentences. Use only the approved sources. Mark any claim that needs a source check with [CHECK].
Rewrite the paragraph below in my voice profile. Keep every fact the same. Don’t add new claims. Cut filler and cliché phrases.
List every factual claim in the draft below: stats, names, dates, quotes, and product features. For each one, tell me what kind of primary source would confirm it. Don’t confirm anything yourself.
Write five meta descriptions of around 150 characters for a post titled “[title]”. Use the primary keyword “[keyword]” once. Promise only what the post delivers.
Below are my draft and a list of related posts with URLs. Suggest up to five places to add internal links. For each, give the sentence, the post, and descriptive anchor text. Only suggest links that truly help the reader.
Use these prompts strategically and flesh them out with your own original thoughts. For more on writing prompts that work, see our guide on how to write AI prompts .
Pro tip: Save your best prompts in a shared doc. Add notes on what each one is good for. Your whole team will get better results, faster.
Google hasn’t explicitly said that it penalizes AI-written content, but its quality standards and spam policy on content abuse at scale target mass-produced pages that add little value for users, regardless of how they’re made. Using AI to generate many pages without adding value is one of its named examples. Publish helpful, accurate, edited posts, and you’re on the right side of that line. For more, see Google’s guidance on generative AI content .
Start with what readers would find useful. Google says sharing how a piece of content was created can give readers helpful context and establish expectations. For example, take “We used AI to help draft this post. Our editors reviewed and fact-checked it.”
Laws are also changing. The EU AI Act’s transparency rules under Article 50 took effect on August 2, 2026, and cover AI-generated text published on matters of public interest, with an exception for text that receives human review or editorial control and is attributed to a person or organization. Whether these rules apply to you depends on your content and audience. Ask your legal team.
Unfortunately, you can’t eliminate AI hallucinations, but you can reduce the risk. Give AI approved sources and tell it to use only those. It may not always listen, but do your due diligence. Draft in small sections. Ask it to mark any claim that needs checking. Then verify every fact yourself.
Hallucinations occur because generative models predict likely words rather than retrieve facts , as Google explains. NIST lists confabulation among the key risks of generative AI . Human review is the safeguard.
Yes, AI can help generate visuals, suggest layouts, or turn your own data into a chart. But never ask it to invent numbers. Build charts from data you can document, and note the source in the caption.
For AI-generated images, add accurate alt text and check the tool’s usage terms. Google also recommends adding image metadata when generating content with automation. Then review every visual the way you’d review any other part of the post.
I can’t say it enough: AI is a tool. It’s a powerful tool, but a tool nevertheless. A hammer can’t build the house, and AI can’t write a great blog post on its own.
Use AI for monotonous things like general info, structuring, outlining, and small repetitive tasks. And save the work that matters most for your people: unique expertise, lived experience, and discernment. That’s what readers want more of, and it’s what AI can’t fake.
Ready to try it? Start drafting with HubSpot’s AI Content Writer , then make every word your own.
